I'll give you the basics. You want to maximise the expected return of your investment while minimising the volatility. The volatility is a measure of how likely it is for the price of your investment to fluctuate. To give you an example, if you could choose between an investment that will get you a 10% return with certainty in a year and another investment that will get you 0% (you lose everything) with probability 50% and 120% return (you get $220 for every $100 invested) with probability 50%, the first investment is better. Both investments have the same expected return (10%), but the first one has lower volatility (zero).

When you buy some sort of investment in the market (shares, bonds, whatever), there's always a trade-off between expected return and volatility. A savings account in a bank, for example, will give you a very low return (below 2% at the moment), but you're guaranteed to get that money. The volatility is virtually zero (I say "virtually" because there's always a very small risk that both the bank and the government that guarantees your deposits will go bust simultaneously or that a giant asteroid will fuck up the planet; nothing's certain in life).

You can, on the other hand, invest in small startups. Most startups are stupid ideas destined to fail, but occasionally you hit the jackpot big time. Startups are very high-risk investments, but the expected values of their returns are also higher than investing in big companies. Coca-Cola or Nike are very unlikely to go out of business, but the trade-off is their dividends will normally not be that great. The bigger and more established the company, the lower the expected return and the lower the volatility.

Is there a way around this? Can you get high returns and low volatility? Yes. Imagine the probability of Coca-Cola going bankrupt in the next 10 years in 10%. If you put all your money on Coca-Cola, you have a 10% chance of losing everything within the next 10 years. Now, if you put 10% of your money on each one of 10 companies as risky as Coca-Cola, the probability that all of them will go bankrup and you will lose all your money is approximately 0.00000001%.

Why approximately? If the risks of those companies going bankrupt were independent, the probability of all of them going bankrupt would be exactly 0.00000001%. Now, those risks are normally not independent. If the ten companies are in Venezuela and a socialist government gets elected, they're all fucked at the same time. Okay, so you just buy stock from companies in different countries, right? Well, no, that's not a guarantee either. If you have stock in 10 different oil companies in 10 different countries and tomorrow somebody invents a method of producing solar panels for 1% of the current cost, you're fucked too. The trick is to diversify your investment into as many different industries and as many different countries as possible. And the good news is you don't need to go throught the hassle of buying hundreds of different stocks from different companies yourself. Some companies already do this for you for a very small commision. The S&P 500, for example, is an "index" of the 500 largest companies in the USA, so if you buy a share in the S&P 500, you're buying into all the 500 largest companies in the USA at the same time. There are many other indices, for other countries and for companies of different sizes. The FTSE 100, for example, is an index of the 100 largest companies in the UK; the Nikkei 225, largest companies in Japan; the Russell 2000 covers small-cap companies in the USA, and so on.

The trick is to be patient. You're not going to become rich overnight. You'll have good years and you'll have bad years. Some years you'll lose money; some other years you'll get returns of 20% or higher. But in the long run you're guaranteed to win; there's no way around it. If this wasn't the case, in 30 years we would have exactly the same technology and the same wealth (or less) we have today, and that's not going to happen.

So that's all you need to do. Pick a few indices from a few different countries, keep putting your money in there, and don't touch it. Don't be tempted to speculate; that's not going to work. You think you're smarter than the market? No, you aren't. Nobody is, not even Warren Buffet. He didn't make money by speculating but by researching companies very thoroughly and then deciding whether they were good investments or not. You don't have the time, resources, or knowledge to do that. That's all you need to know.
